verdicts.evidence: The audit runs audit_metric_identities.py evaluating the supporting-score identity for L1, L2, and KL on a 99×100 grid, yielding max oracle identity error 0, max constant-target score 0, and max supporting-plane violation 1.11e-16, confirming the mathematical foundation of all three ERT metrics.

Re-aggregation of the authors' pinned results.csv (5,600 rows) yields LightGBM relative L1 power 68.929% vs PartitionWise 33.671% (2.05× ratio), closely matching the paper's LightGBM figure of 68.4% and strongly supporting the qualitative claim, though the PartitionWise value differs from the paper's 38.3%, likely due to released-code updates.

Independent synthetic experiment on the paper's 8D heteroscedastic model (3,000 calibration samples, up to 30,000 test points) shows L1-ERT recovering 92% of the analytic violation (0.0866 vs 0.0948) at 30k points, while unaligned CovGap recovers only 5% (0.0049), with oracle-group CovGap working well (0.0953).

The same 30,000-point synthetic run estimates over-coverage at 0.0445 (analytic 0.0460) and under-coverage at 0.0464 (analytic 0.0488), both nonzero and close to theory, confirming the asymmetric decomposition separates over- and under-coverage.

Reading all 80 rows of the official classification CSV confirms the additive identity (max residual 8.94e-8) and shows all 8 dataset/method groups have directional KL-ERT gaps above 0.01 (e.g., CIFAR100/cumulative: 0.0160 vs 0.1745), demonstrating divergent over/under-coverage components in practice.

A controlled experiment with 20 seeds, 2,000 observations, and 5 folds shows a label memorizer produces false in-sample L2-ERT of 0.08886 but zero cross-fitted ERT, while a genuine two-region signal is still detected (0.01013), with maximum train/evaluation overlap of 0, confirming k-fold cross-fitting prevents overfitting without erasing real signal.

overall: The logbook provides concrete evidence for all six claims through a mix of independent experiments (Claims 1, 3, 4, 6) and deterministic re-aggregations of the authors' hash-pinned released outputs (Claims 2, 5). The independent synthetic experiments use the paper's actual 8D heteroscedastic model at meaningful sample sizes, and the released-output replays are transparently distinguished from fresh training runs.
